name: Olmec
summary: Often called the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica, famous for colossal stone heads. Whether it was the origin of later cultures is debated.

knownFor.label: Colossal heads
knownFor.note: Huge basalt heads, probably portraits of rulers.

knownFor.label: Jade carving
knownFor.note: Fine carved jade figures and masks.

knownFor.label: Mesoamerican ballgame
knownFor.note: Rubber balls show the game was played very early.

location.value: The Gulf Coast lowlands of Mexico (Veracruz and Tabasco).

terrain.value: Tropical lowlands with rivers (the Coatzacoalcos basin) and well-watered alluvial soil.

climate.value: Hot and humid tropical lowlands of the Gulf Coast.
climate.source: Diehl, The Olmecs: America’s First Civilization (2004)

resources.value: Fertile river soil for maize. Jade, obsidian and magnetite were obtained from far away.

disasters.value: Environmental changes (shifting rivers, siltation, possibly volcanism) are suggested causes of decline.

population.value: Not known. The population of the eastern heartland dropped sharply between 400 and 350 BCE.

urbanisation.value: Ceremonial centres: San Lorenzo (to about 900 BCE), then La Venta (900–400 BCE), and Tres Zapotes.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: People dispersed when the centres were abandoned. The culture continued as the Epi-Olmec.

economicBase.value: Farming (maize, beans, squash, cassava) and fishing.

tradeRoutes.value: Long-distance exchange of jade (from Guatemala), obsidian and magnetite.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; jade and ritual objects show a wealthy elite.

moneyAndTax.value: No money is known. Elites controlled valuable goods and labour.
moneyAndTax.source: Diehl, The Olmecs: America’s First Civilization (2004)

inequality.value: A hierarchical society: moving a colossal head may have taken about 1,500 people for months.

governmentType.value: Probably chiefdoms or early states led by rulers with religious authority.
governmentType.source: Diehl, The Olmecs: America’s First Civilization (2004)

keyRulers.value: No names are known. The colossal heads are probably portraits of rulers.

succession.value: Unknown; colossal heads may show hereditary rulers.

institutions.value: Elite and religious leadership organising monument building.
institutions.source: Diehl, The Olmecs: America’s First Civilization (2004)

stability.value: Shifts of power from San Lorenzo (abandoned about 900 BCE) to La Venta.

armyAndTech.value: Little evidence. There was probably no standing army.

inventions.value: Monumental stone carving and rubber balls (from at least 1600 BCE). Possibly early writing (the Cascajal Block) and the Long Count calendar; both are disputed.

scienceEducation.value: Possibly early writing and calendrics. The evidence is debated.

openness.value: Interacted widely across Mesoamerica through trade in jade and obsidian.

religion.value: Rulers and shamans held religious roles. Were-jaguar imagery, a feathered serpent, and ritual bloodletting.

languageWriting.value: Language unknown (a Mixe–Zoquean link is debated). Name from the Nahuatl “rubber people”.

artsArchitecture.value: 17 colossal basalt heads (up to 3.4 m, 25–55 tonnes), jade carvings, and La Venta’s Great Pyramid (34 m), the largest Mesoamerican structure of its time.

socialStructure.value: Rulers and elites above farmers and craftsmen.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared art style and religious symbols.
sharedIdentity.source: Diehl, The Olmecs: America’s First Civilization (2004)

neighbours.value: Other Formative Mesoamerican peoples, in Oaxaca, Guerrero and the Maya region.

ideasReligions.value: Often called the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica: the ballgame, bloodletting and artistic motifs spread to later cultures. This is debated.

riseSignals.value: Fertile river land, elite control of exotic goods, and religious authority. Origins go back to at least 1600–1500 BCE.

peakPeriod.value: San Lorenzo (c. 1200–900 BCE), then La Venta (900–400 BCE).

declineSignals.value: Possibly environmental changes (rivers, siltation, volcanism). The cause is unknown.

outcome.value: The major centres were abandoned by about 400 BCE. The Epi-Olmec culture continued at Tres Zapotes.

sources.value: Archaeology only (no readable texts). Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Diehl (2004).

overallCertainty.value: Low. Dates vary (Wikipedia gives c. 1200–400 BCE, or from 1400 BCE). Language, politics and causes of decline are unknown. Second source: Wikidata starts c. 1400 BCE; this app uses c. 1200 BCE.
